title: Senior's toolkit: addresses, ports and captures
summary: What is my address, who listens on which port, can I reach it, and what is actually on the wire: the commands for each.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: addresses, ports and captures
steps.body: Most network tickets start with three questions: which address am I on, is anything listening, and does the packet actually leave? These commands answer each one in seconds.

toolkit.what: Every interface with its state and addresses, one line each. The modern replacement for `ifconfig`, which most distros no longer install.
Which processes listen on which TCP and UDP ports, and on which address. Replaces `netstat`.
flags: the owning process (sudo to see other users')

toolkit.what: Which process has port 8080 open, listening or connected. Good for finding the stray dev server that holds a port.
Test that a TCP port answers, without sending any data. The quickest "is the firewall open?" check from the client side.
The Windows equivalent of `nc -zv`: resolves the name, tries the TCP port and reports `TcpTestSucceeded`.
flags: just True or False, for scripts

toolkit.what: Show the packets on the wire. Proves whether traffic arrives at all, and whether the other side answers or resets.
flags: a capture filter: keep only what you need
toolkit.example: sudo tcpdump -i any -nn -c 50 host 10.0.0.5 and port 5432

toolkit.what: Save a capture to a file and open it later in Wireshark, which decodes every protocol and follows TCP streams.
flags: rotate: five files of 100 MB, so a long capture cannot fill the disk

steps.prompt: Match each command to the question it answers.
pairs: which addresses does this machine have?
what is listening, and on which address?
can I open a TCP connection to the database?
are packets for port 443 really arriving?

steps.prompt: Capture HTTPS traffic on every interface, without name lookups, into a file you can open in Wireshark.
steps.explain: `-i any` listens on every interface, `-nn` skips DNS and port-name lookups (which also keeps tcpdump from generating its own DNS traffic), and `-w` writes raw packets. `-r` is for reading a file back.

steps.prompt: `dotnet run` fails with `Failed to bind to address http://127.0.0.1:5000: address already in use`. What do you run first?
options: `sudo ss -tlnp 'sport = :5000'` (or `lsof -nP -i :5000`) to see which process holds the port
steps.explain: Something already listens on 5000, often an older run of the same app or another service. `ss -p` or `lsof` names the process and its PID; then stop it or pick another port.

steps.prompt: The app logs `connection timed out` to `10.0.3.7:5432`. On the database host, `tcpdump -i any -nn port 5432` shows nothing while the app retries. What does that tell you?
options: The packets never reach the database host: look at routing, security groups or a firewall in between
steps.explain: A stopped service or a loopback-only bind would make the host answer with a reset (seen in tcpdump, and the client gets "refused"). Silence on the server side means the SYN is dropped before it arrives.

steps.prompt: A client cannot reach your service on port 8443. Work from the server outwards.
lines: sudo ss -tlnp 'sport = :8443'   # is it listening, and on 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1?
curl -vk https://localhost:8443/health   # does it answer locally?
nc -zv -w 3 server 8443   # from the client: does the port open?
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn port 8443   # on the server: do the client's packets arrive?
also: sudo ss -tlnp 'sport = :8443'   # is it listening, and on 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1?
curl -vk https://localhost:8443/health   # does it answer locally?
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn port 8443   # on the server: do the client's packets arrive?
nc -zv -w 3 server 8443   # from the client: does the port open?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When something "cannot connect", check listening (`ss -tlnp`), then reachability (`nc -zv`), then the wire (`tcpdump`) before you touch any config. Paste the outputs into the ticket: they turn "the network is broken" into a fact someone can act on.
